title: Kamsa Orders the Gopas Expelled and Vasudeva Punished
story:
The last wrestler had fallen, and the arena lay quiet. One by one Kamsa's champions had gone down — Chanura and Toshala, whom Krishna had thrown down and struck; Mushtika and Andhra, whom Balarama had brought down with fists like a thundercloud. The great wrestling ground, so lately roaring, now stood empty of fighters, and the crowd began to understand what it was watching.

High above them sat the king of Mathura, and his face ran with sweat. Kamsa had matched the two brothers against his finest wrestlers in the arena, and now, one after another, his champions lay still. The painted lines on his brow were washing away in perspiration, and his lips trembled with a rage that had nowhere left to go. Every breath fed the fire of his fear and his hatred until the two became one burning thing.

So Kamsa did what a cornered tyrant does. He turned on the helpless.

He raised his voice to his guards, and the words fell on the assembly like a sentence. Turn out of the arena these two sinful, grim-faced young cowherds from the forest, he said. I do not wish to see them. None of the cowherds deserves to remain in my territory. Then he pointed at Nanda, the old chief of the cowherds, the man who had raised Krishna as his own. This Nanda is wicked, Kamsa said, and bent on doing me harm — bind him with chains and spikes of iron. And Vasudeva, his own kinsman: Vasudeva is wicked too, he said; punish him this very day in a manner no aged man deserves. The rest of the cowherds, he added, are all devoted to Krishna; strip them of their cattle and their wealth.

It was not enough that the king had tried to kill the brothers. He reached now for everyone who loved them — the father who had raised them, the father who had begotten them, the whole community that had come up from Vraja to see them. The cruelty lay in how precisely it was aimed. He knew exactly where to wound.

Across the arena, Vasudeva heard the sentence passed on himself and on Nanda, and he fixed Kamsa with a long, unblinking gaze; his strength was truth, and he did not flinch. But Krishna saw it all at once — his father Vasudeva insulted, Nanda insulted, his kinsmen in distress, and Devaki fallen senseless at the sight — and something in him turned. The wrath that rose was not the hot anger of a boy. It was the gathered anger of everything that had been done to his people, and it had found its object at last.

Kamsa's hour had come, though Kamsa could not see it. The king sat there possessed by his own doom, unable to look plainly at the man before him. And Krishna, with the speed of a lion, began to leap across the arena toward the king's pavilion, to put an end to the man who had spent his whole life trying to kill him.
reflection: Kamsa's rage, once his champions fail him, does not collapse into despair; it turns outward and downward, onto the defenseless — the foster father, the kinsman, the whole community. The story marks the precise moment a tyrant stops even pretending to rule and simply lashes out, and it marks Krishna's wrath as the answer that such a man has made inevitable.
tradition_note: This telling follows the Harivamsha, where the provocation that immediately precedes Kamsa's death is his order to expel the cowherds, bind Nanda, and punish Vasudeva.
hero_scene: Kamsa, face flushed and dripping with sweat, rising in fury in his pavilion to point at Nanda and Vasudeva as he orders the cowherds expelled, while Krishna below him begins to leap across the empty arena with the speed of a lion.
visual_elements: Kamsa on his high seat, sweating and enraged
a mood of tyranny breaking against wrath
